Replayable Authority Histories for Auditing Automated Agents (https://www.ietf.org/ietf-ftp/internet-drafts/draft-rampertab-audit-agent-authority-history-00.html)
【turn169099view0】 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://www.ietf.org/ietf-ftp/internet-drafts/draft-rampertab-audit-agent-authority-history-00.html","lineno":527}); Total lines: 1047
L514: A reader reconstructs state by replaying every record from genesis under the profile's fixed check order; the profile MUST specify chain, schema, authorization, transition and capacity precedence. A rejected record leaves the state unchanged, the rejection names the position, and a history containing a rejected record is invalid as a whole.
L515: Given the same history, request and evaluation time, every conforming implementation MUST produce the same decision, proof and evidence list; evaluation time is an explicit input, never the reader's clock, and evidence lists MUST be ordered deterministically. A specification instantiating this model SHOULD publish conformance vectors and SHOULD have at least two independent implementations pass them; passing a finite set is bounded evidence, not universal correctness.【331†¶】
L516: ### 【68†5.5.】 【69†Evidence references】
L517: Every claim a decision or query makes MUST be supported by an evidence reference naming a record by identifier, type, position and history hash. Further kinds MAY name an authority by its grant record, a credential by its admission, a receipt by content hash and record, or an external attestation by type, reference and attester. Evidence is bounded; a result whose evidence would exceed the bound is INDETERMINATE with an explicit code, never silently truncated.【332†¶】
L518: ### 【70†5.6.】 【71†State commitment】
L519: A conforming encoding MUST define a state root committing to the complete set of state records at a position, such that matching roots commit to matching record sets. Inclusion needs a verified path, leaf index and tree size; sorted non-membership additionally needs authenticated adjacent indices and boundary proofs and an authenticated commitment whose ordering and uniqueness were validated; two arbitrary inclusion paths are insufficient.
L520: A Merkle tree over the sorted state records in the manner of [【215†RFC6962】] satisfies this. An instantiation MUST support owner-signed checkpoints and root-bearing head attestations, distinguishing the state before a checkpoint from the state including it. A reader resuming from a cache MUST recompute the root and compare it with an owner-signed root at exactly that position, falling back to full replay on mismatch; a mismatch alone does not establish owner-key misuse.
L521: A signed starting state is an owner assertion unless independently replayed.【333†¶】
L522: ## 【72†6.】 【73†Decisions and refusals】
L523: ### 【74†6.1.】 【75†The decision procedure】
L524: 
L525: A request names an actor, an action, a resource and a claimed time, and optionally an amount, a counterparty and a commitment to terms. A decision is one of the results in 【334†Table 11】.【335†¶】
L526: 【336†Table 11】: 【337†The three decision results】
L527: Result  | Meaning  | Carries
L528: --- | --- | ---
L529: ALLOW  | Authority exists  | A proof: the root, the permission path from root to actor, intersections satisfied, effective constraints after attenuation, the controlling authority identifiers, usage snapshot of every capped grant, authority evidence, prohibitions checked
L530: DENY  | Authority does not exist or is overridden  | A code and a sorted list of failures with evidence. Codes MUST at least distinguish: action not allowed, no authority, revoked, expired, not yet valid, prohibited, agent inactive, session fenced, missing intersection, amount exceeded
L531: INDETERMINATE  | The history or request cannot support a decision (unverifiable relation, invalid causal time, evidence over the bound)  | A code and evidence. MUST NOT be treated as ALLOW; an enforcement point that must choose MUST treat it as a refusal
L532: The procedure MUST evaluate, in order: domain and policy identifiers; causal time (evaluation time not before the head's time); the actor's lifecycle; the session binding when the request is consequential; candidate permission paths from recognized roots; delegation status along each path; required intersections; prohibitions; per-grant limits including cumulative usage. Budgets (【259†Section 6.3】) are consulted only after an ALLOW and can only turn it into a DENY.
L533: Every result MUST state, as constant values, that it is a reading of the captured history and not a capability to execute anything.【338†¶】
L534: ### 【76†6.2.】 【77†Consequential requests and admissions】
L535: A request intended for consequential execution is consequential. The runtime declares an intent (actor, action, resource, role and tenure, the adapter that will carry it out, optional amount, counterparty and terms commitment, and a nonce); the engine records an admission carrying the evaluation time, the expected head and the proof.
L536: After an admission the record may show a consumption (the adapter's signed acknowledgment), an outcome (confirmed, failed, disputed or unknown), a receipt (a compact artifact checkable against a supplied prefix), and effects (measurements reported by a session, connector or counterparty). None establishes that the world changed; each establishes that a signer claimed something at a head.
L537: A job with an uncertain submission stays outcome-unknown until reconciled; exactly-once effects require executor idempotency and recovery, which a signed history cannot supply by itself.【339†¶】
L538: ### 【78†6.3.】 【79†Budgets】
L539: 
L540: An instantiation MUST support budgets: owner-declared stop rules over a group of requests selected by actors, roles, actions, resources and metric, with a cap per period, per operation or in count, and bounded carry-over. A budget selected by role MUST follow the role across a handover. Budgets are charged by admissions only, never by refusals or effects; a matching selector alone does not meter effects.【340†¶】
L541: ### 【80†6.4.】 【81†Refusals as records】
L542: 
L543: A conforming history MUST support a refusal record, session-signed, with the fields in 【341†Table 12】.【342†¶】
L544: 【343†Table 12】: 【344†The refusal record】
L545: Field  | Rule
L546: --- | ---
L547: Source  | The authority procedure (CORE), a budget, or a connector (an enforcement point outside the engine)
L548: Request  | As evaluated
L549: Evaluation time  | MUST equal the record's timestamp
L550: Expected head  | MUST be the head immediately before the record
L551: Decision and code  | DENY or INDETERMINATE; the budget identifier for a budget refusal; connector identifier, code and detail digest for a connector refusal
L552: Signer  | For CORE and budget refusals the signing session's agent MUST be the request's actor; for a connector refusal, the connector's own admitted agent
L553: For CORE and budget refusals, replay MUST re-run the decision on the state before the record and MUST reject the record unless decision, code and budget identifier are reproduced; a refusal the state would have allowed is a replay rejection. A connector refusal is attested, not re-derived: the engine cannot reproduce a decision it did not make.
L554: A reproduced DENY establishes the recorded denial at that head; INDETERMINATE establishes that the inputs could not support ALLOW; an attested refusal proves only that an admitted connector claimed to have refused. An expired, fenced, terminated or never-admitted actor cannot sign its own CORE or budget refusal; a live connector session can attest the mapped attempt instead.【345†¶】
L555: Refusals never change usage counters. A writer SHOULD coalesce identical refusals per actor within a short window and SHOULD rate-limit them, and MUST report whether a refusal was recorded and, if not, why; the history therefore need not enumerate every attempt. A deployment that wants refusals enforced as well as recorded MUST place the decision point where the action is executed (【346†Section 10.1】).【347†¶】
L556: ## 【82†7.】 【83†Counterparty receipts and external policy】
L557: ### 【84†7.1.】 【85†Counterparty receipts】
L558: An instantiation MUST support owner-authorized registration and retirement of counterparty verification keys and session-recorded counterparty receipts, distinguishing a local issuer receipt, a commitment to an artifact, and a separately counterparty-signed artifact; a digest alone MUST NOT be reported as authenticated counterparty evidence.
L559: A receipt MUST bind the history identity, counterparty and key, the earlier admitted intent and its declaration digest, and the reported effect and time; its wrapper MUST bind the recording session and preceding head. Replay MUST require an ACTIVE counterparty with the named key at the wrapper position and verify the envelope signature before the wrapper authorization. Retirement MUST NOT invalidate an earlier accepted wrapper; new wrappers during retirement MUST be rejected.

L633: An instantiation MUST expose separate read-only inspection, authorization evaluation and controlled write interfaces. CLI, SDK, Model Context Protocol (MCP) and agent-framework bindings are application interfaces, not authority sources; an authenticated caller binding MUST map a connection to the configured actor, session and tenure; untrusted caller parameters MUST NOT select another actor's privilege; and read-only handles MUST NOT become execution capabilities.
L634: A protected-resource profile MUST identify the trusted host, custody and access boundary; restoration requires separate authorization and MUST NOT discharge the investigation duty. A service MUST bound its resources, capture one consistent observation per composite query and apply an explicit disclosure policy; a natural-language explanation interface MUST retain the typed result and evidence links and MUST NOT upgrade an unverified conclusion.
L635: A durable-job interface MUST persist an opaque handle bound to the original attempt before launch, check caller access and permission on every poll, inspection or cancellation, and MUST NOT infer an effect retry from reconnection; a handle MUST NOT confer authority, and a cancellation acknowledgment MUST distinguish stopping later outgoing phases from cancellation at the destination and from rollback of an applied effect.
L636: An authenticated HTTP binding MUST validate issuer, audience, token type and lifetime, MUST reject token-supplied discovery keys or URLs outside the configured trust policy, MUST NOT forward bearer credentials upstream or retain them in records, MUST recheck caller access around asynchronous signing, dispatch and disclosure, and MUST NOT interpret a disconnect, expired token or refusal as cancellation or proof of no effect. A public service profile MUST specify HTTPS and custody boundaries.
L637: Access loss after an effect MUST preserve the attempt while withholding disclosure under current policy.【368†¶】
L638: ## 【108†10.】 【109†Reconciliation】
L639: ### 【110†10.1.】 【111†Why a decision point is not enough】
L640: No decision point sees every call: a host may execute a tool without asking, a sub-agent may run without the hook, a script may call a service directly, and a token the agent holds may be used outside any gate. A history that records only what passed through the decision point proves what the decision point saw and decided, not what the agent did.
L641: A deployment claiming coverage under this model MUST publish an assessed coverage table (scope, version, period, assessor, known unknowns) classifying every identified effect path as in 【369†Table 15】. A claim that an agent is "governed" without this table is not supported by the model.【370†¶】
L642: 【371†Table 15】: 【372†Coverage classes for an effect path】
L643: Class  | Meaning
L644: --- | ---
L645: enforced  | The decision point both decides and performs, or holds the only credentials, with assessed controls that prevent the effect on DENY: credential isolation, protected executors, stale-decision checks, fail-closed behavior. Holding a credential on a hostile host is insufficient
L646: recorded  | The effect can occur without a decision, but an observation feed with documented coverage and loss guarantees is reconciled against the history (【373†Section 10.2】)
L647: open  | Neither enforced nor observed
L648: ### 【112†10.2.】 【113†Reconciliation observations】
L649: An instantiation MUST support RECONCILIATION_OBSERVED as a session-signed finding. The signer MUST be an admitted session whose agent equals the recorded reconciler; an owner signature MUST NOT be accepted in its place.
L650: Each observation MUST carry a unique identifier, the reconciler, the source stream and event reference with a digest, the observed call fields with explicit unsupplied-field markers under profile-defined optional-field and absence rules, a MATCHED or UNMATCHED result, the immediately preceding head, the session binding and a purpose-specific signature.
L651: A MATCHED reference MUST identify an earlier admission or refusal whose actor equals the observed actor; a match to a refusal MUST NOT be treated as permission or as an effect claim, and the verifier MUST list fields that differ from the matched request and observations whose reconciler equals the observed actor.【374†¶】
L652: A later observation whose digest equals an accepted one for the same stream and reference MUST be rejected as a duplicate; one whose digest differs, if accepted, MUST carry an equivocation reference to the earliest, which verification lists without invalidating the history. Replay MUST validate schema, session authorization with its fence precedence, reconciler binding and preceding head, then the match and duplicate rules, before capacity.
L653: Replay MUST NOT infer provider completeness or re-create undisclosed source bytes from the digest; a cursor keyed by reconciler and stream MUST track the last accepted reference, and opaque source references MUST NOT be assumed ordered. Under the writer lock the writer MUST match at the append head, sign and durably append before advancing its collection checkpoint, recovering a crash through the original source identity without recording twice.
L654: A verifier MUST present unmatched, equivocation and mismatch listings as signer claims about supplied feed events: they prove neither complete coverage nor an external effect. Legacy ledger migration MUST append each observation at the current head and MUST NOT back-date history records. Collection intervals, feed loss and matching criteria MUST be reported as deployment evidence.【375†¶】
L655: ## 【114†11.】 【115†Export, verification and freshness】
L656: ### 【116†11.1.】 【117†The export view】
L657: An export MUST carry at least: the domain, the concrete profile identifier, authenticated history identity and the genesis event hash, distinguished from the genesis record-chain hash; the heads at both ends of the range; every record in the range with its hash; every owner key rotation at or before the end; where state roots are defined, the roots at both ends, the full state at the start and audit paths for requested records; the owner attestations and witness receipts held for both heads; and the dependency closure of earlier bodies read by transitions.
L658: A verifier MUST authenticate its trust anchors and identity first, then signatures and transitions. A later starting state requires full prefix replay or an authenticated starting-root commitment, and the export MUST report starting-state authentication separately from transition validity.【376†¶】
L659: ### 【118†11.2.】 【119†What a verifier establishes】
L660: Given an export and the owner public keys, a verifier that trusts neither agent nor operator can establish: chain integrity; control-record authenticity (every change of power satisfies the policy in force, bound to position and effect); session-record authenticity under each type's rules; decision reproduction (every admission was authorized at the head it names and every CORE or budget refusal reproduces); captured authority at any position and explicit evaluation time; refusals, including which were attested rather than reproduced; duties and handovers, including that no grant followed; reported observations with their results; state equality where an owner-signed root is available; and, where selected, human-eligibility evidence against the named policy.【377†¶】
L661: It does not establish that an action had its effect in the world, that every call passed through the decision point, that timestamps are true, that an owner key was held by the right person, or that the export is the latest state unless freshness evidence from outside the host is available (【378†Table 2】).【379†¶】
L662: ### 【120†11.3.】 【121†Rollback and freshness: local anchors, witnesses and public chains】
L663: 
L664: Chain hashing cannot distinguish a history from the same history with a valid suffix removed. 【380†Table 16】 lists the mechanisms, from a file beside the history to a public chain; they differ in who must be compromised to roll the history back undetected.【381†¶】
L665: 【382†Table 16】: 【383†Freshness mechanisms, weakest to strongest】
L666: Mechanism  | Where the evidence lives  | Defeats  | Does not defeat
L667: --- | --- | --- | ---
L668: Head attestation  | A file beside the history, written after each owner-attested write  | Truncation by anyone who cannot rewrite the attestation  | An operator who restores an older copy with its older genuine attestation

L756: Coerced or colluding attester  | Attest an agent-held key as human, or refuse renewal  | Statements inert until the owner quorum embeds them; two attesters required; the quorum removes attester and statement by policy rotation; lapsed keys keep power reduction, checkpoints and restoration  | Collusion between quorum and attester is indistinguishable from consent; with no cooperating attester, keys, attesters, thresholds and floor stay frozen
L757: Witness or witness-key thief  | Withhold replies or serve disjoint views  | Pinned keys, nonce/deadline, inclusion/consistency checks, remembered checkpoints and independent comparison  | A nonce alone does not stop split views; unsubmitted work is invisible
L758: Provider/counterparty  | Omit, rewrite or fabricate reports  | Retain digest/issuer evidence, list equivocation and match differences  | Signatures authenticate the reporter, not effect or complete coverage
L759: Reconciler  | Mis-map calls, omit observations, self-observe  | Admitted-session binding, explicit absent fields, source identity, duplicate/equivocation lists  | No completeness theorem; matching actor alone does not establish execution binding
L760: External decider/destination  | Change policy, disappear, return stale results  | Same-request policy binding, fail-closed required policy, acknowledged fence/status recovery  | Cross-service atomicity and full destination rollback require a stronger profile
L761: Anchor publisher or chain-facing RPC  | Withhold or misreport publication; submit a stale or conflicting commitment  | Authenticate chain/profile and intended history; validate execution, finality and committed-prefix continuity; retain independent checkpoints  | Unpublished work/forks remain invisible; fees, outage and stale bootstrap can stop freshness
L762: Federation member or coordinator  | Propose invalid order/state, withhold bodies, equivocate or censor  | Independent deterministic replay, authenticated membership/quorum, actual post-state commitment evidence and retained bodies  | Corrupt quorum, common administration, unavailable evidence or unsafe membership change can defeat the profile
L763: Dispatcher or former leader  | Repeat an external call or execute after authority changes  | Fresh effect-boundary checks, committed attempt identity, leadership fencing and downstream idempotency/status  | Consensus alone supplies neither external atomicity nor exactly-once effects
L764: Agent using a human's device or key  | Reuse enrolled credentials, automate prompts or sign after unlock  | Exact-key enrollment binding; qualified custody; fresh action approval where required  | Enrollment alone does not prove current human participation; an unlocked/exported key can be misused
L765: Dishonest voucher or Sybil ring  | Certify fabricated relationships or agent-controlled keys  | Authenticated bootstrap, another-person checks, scoped signed vouches, diversity and prospective status handling  | Colluding roots or real humans can lie; distinct keys are not necessarily distinct people
L766: Coercer or deepfake attacker  | Manipulate the subject or impersonate live interaction  | Independent contact, context-bound live checks, in-person option and incident recovery  | No biometric/signature proves voluntary intent; remote presence tests remain fallible
L767: Authenticator or attestation issuer compromise  | Falsify biometric/key-protection evidence  | Qualified method-specific profiles, pinned metadata/trust and status evidence, re-attestation  | Verification still depends on the device, issuer and assessment process
L768: Registry/status operator  | Hide revocation, replay old good status or correlate subjects  | Committed historical cutoffs, current freshness checks, private evidence, independent checkpoints  | Availability and unseen later status remain separate; hashes may still enable correlation
L769: The cryptographic basis is: chain hashing for integrity within the record; owner signatures over position and effect for every change of power; type-specific session signatures; re-derivation of non-migrated admissions and CORE/BUDGET refusals on replay, while CONNECTOR, reconciliation and external-decider findings remain signer claims; and, for freshness, owner-attested heads held outside the host.【417†¶】
L770: ### 【134†14.2.】 【135†The host is trusted by the engine, not by the verifier】
L771: The engine runs inside the host with the host's permissions; a host can skip the check, patch the clock or read key files. The model confines what the host can do undetected rather than pretend otherwise. Unhooked calls are not seen (【346†Section 10.1】); a verifier assessing a completeness claim MUST obtain and report the coverage table. A decision is point-in-time.
L772: History time is the writers' claim: a clock set forward expires grants early, a clock set backward is caught only when it would precede the head. Deployments SHOULD use a monotone, trusted clock, readers SHOULD refuse a head unreasonably ahead of their own clock, and where grants and budgets depend on time a deployment SHOULD identify a trusted-time or witness-receipt-time binding and its uncertainty. A single signer's control over time is bounded only as 【242†Section 4.6】 states.
L773: A session key has similar control. A session record carries a timestamp chosen by its signer. Replay rejects it if that time is at or past the session's expiry, and, under the attested floor, at or past the expiry of an owner attestation that was still valid at the preceding head (【418†Section 4.3】). Someone who steals a session key and can add records directly can therefore move history time forward to just before the earlier of those limits.
L774: Advancing the epoch stops further records but does not move time back. Deployments SHOULD accept session records only through their own writer, which checks each timestamp against the deployment's trusted clock; a verifier cannot tell afterwards whether that writer was used.
L775: A history whose genesis sets a session-time horizon (【418†Section 4.3】) bounds this in replay itself: a session key can then move history time no further than that horizon past the time of the latest owner-signed record that advanced history time. The cost is operational: once the horizon is reached, sessions cannot record until an owner writes such a record, so an unattended deployment needs scheduled owner records and therefore an owner key that is available.【419†¶】
L776: ### 【136†14.3.】 【137†Key compromise】
L777: 【420†Table 20】: 【421†Key compromise】
L778: Key  | What its thief can do  | Response  | Limit
L779: --- | --- | --- | ---
L780: Owner (enough to meet the policy)  | Produce valid control records and attestations  | Rotation; pre-rotation keeps a thief holding only current keys from locking the owner out, provided the committed key is kept off the host  | Signatures establish which keys signed, not who authorized; one key suffices in a single-key profile; a retired key still signs a copy cut back to before its rotation, and only later-head evidence tells that copy from the real one
L781: Committed next key  | Under recovery, co-sign the revealing rotation; otherwise freeze the set by withholding  | Custody as a current key; rotation threshold of two with distinct custodians  | Under a threshold of one, its holder takes the history alone; the threshold counts keys, not custodians
L782: Session  | Sign admissions, refusals, receipts and duties until expiry or epoch advance; advance history time up to its expiry, the next owner-attestation expiry under the attested floor, or a set session-time horizon past the latest time-advancing owner-signed record, if its records bypass the deployment's writer (【206†Section 14.2】)  | Epoch advance, which bypasses declared limits; finite session expiry  | Can still fail at absolute caps or on unavailable storage
L783: Witness  | Equivocate: show different logs to different clients  | Remembered checkpoints; several independent witnesses  | Cannot forge owner statements or alter contents it never sees
L784: Reconciler session  | Mis-map or omit observations  | Admitted-session binding, listing rules  | Admission does not certify honesty or independence
L785: Chain publisher, validator, dispatcher  | Stall progress or publish invalid commitments; repeat a call  | Verifiers check validity and prefix continuity; committee fault threshold; fencing and idempotency  | None can forge owner authorization; a hidden fork stays hidden

About the security of the 1Password Account Trust Log | 1Password Support (https://support.1password.com/account-trust-log-security/)
【turn169099view3】 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://support.1password.com/account-trust-log-security/","lineno":68}); Total lines: 179
L36: The Trust Log records how the account changes over time, while the World State is a snapshot of all trusted data at a moment in time. Each entry stores its World State’s integrity value, so the two structures stay tightly coupled.
L37: 
L38: The following are some important properties of the World State:
L39: 
L40:   * A complete Trust Log can always be replayed, entry by entry, to reconstruct a World State.
L41:   * The World State has a canonical form: Each Trust Log entry corresponds to exactly one World State.
L42: The World State is implemented as a 【3†Modified Patricia-Merkle Trie (MPT)†ethereum.org】, which is a type of 【4†radix trie.†en.wikipedia.org】 MPTs fit this use case because they’re efficient to store and query, while also being deterministic, verifiable, and flexible in what they store.
L43: ## Appending to the Trust Log
L44: 
L45: An easy way to understand the Trust Log as a verifiable chain is to see how a new entry is built and appended.
L46: ### Entry structure
L47: 
L48: Each Trust Log entry includes the following:
L49: 
L50:   * Operation: The change the entry makes to the World State.
L51:   * Entry integrity: A hash of the previous entry in the chain.
L52:   * Signature: Authentication of who created the entry.
L53:   * Metadata: Extra context about the entry.
L54: 
L55: Because each new entry includes the previous entry’s hash, clients can verify the full history. Changing any entry invalidates the integrity of every later entry, so tampering is detectable.
L56: ### Appending a new entry
L57: 
L58: Appending starts from the latest Trust Log entry (HEAD) and its World State:
L59: 
L60: 【5†Image: A diagram showing the latest entry in the Trust Log and its World State.】
L61: 
L62: A new Operation is built from the action being performed. The rules for how an Operation updates the World State are precise and shared by all clients. Applying the Operation to the current World State yields the new World State and its integrity value:
L63: 【6†Image: A diagram showing the path from the action in the Trust Log to the current World State and the new World State based on the operation.】
L64: Using the new World State integrity, the HEAD’s integrity, and other metadata, the new entry is assembled. The inclusion of the HEAD entry’s integrity makes sure that the new entry forms a new link in the chain of the Trust Log. The contents of the new entry will be used by clients to make sure the entry was a valid operation at the time it was created and hasn’t been tampered with since.
L65: The new entry is serialized, signed, and sent to the server to append to the account’s Trust Log and distribute to everyone on the account:
L66: 
L67: 【7†Image: A diagram showing the path from the new entry to the latest entry, then the World State.】
L68: ### Client verification
L69: 
L70: As the Trust Log grows, each client must track the account’s current trusted state. Updating local state to match the latest shared log is called fast-forwarding.
L71: 
L72: Fast-forwarding verifies each new entry in order. Besides basic structure checks, clients must make sure:
L73:   1. The entry’s signature is valid and belongs to a key present in the World State.
L74:   2. The entry contains a valid reference to the integrity value of the previous entry in the log.
L75:   3. The entry number is exactly one greater than the previous entry’s number.
L76: 
L77: Only after every entry passes these checks can the client trust the account state described by the latest World State.
L78: 
L79: The server has two primary functions:
L80:   1. Data consistency: It makes sure that all submitters are up to date and new entries append to a single, sequential, shared chain (one Trust Log per account).
L81:   2. Governance: It enforces existing access control mechanisms, which makes sure that only users with the correct permissions within the account can append corresponding operations to the Trust Log.
L82: ### Syncing and bookmarks
L83: 
L84: On multiple devices, users can avoid re-verifying Trust Log segments they’ve already checked by using a Bookmark.
L85: 
L86: A Bookmark records how far into the Trust Log a user has verified. Because the log is append-only, verified history doesn’t need to be re-checked. Bookmarks are a safe starting point when fast-forwarding: You trust the log up to that point because you’ve already verified earlier entries.
L87: Bookmarks are signed with a key derived from the user’s symmetric key, so they stay authentic even when stored somewhere untrusted (for example, on the server). One client can upload a Bookmark, then another can fetch and verify it with the same user symmetric key.
L88: To maintain trust on first use, clients also store a Bookmark locally so the server can’t falsely claim there’s no Trust Log. When someone joins an account or sees the Trust Log for the first time (for example, first sign-in after enablement), they have no Bookmark yet and must implicitly trust the server’s claim about the latest entry to create their first Bookmark. After that, they can detect later server tampering.
L89: ### Server entries
L90: 
L91: The Trust Log is meant to limit server interference, but some features require the server to change account state without a user signing an entry (for example, the account policy to 【8†automatically delete suspended users】). The server must be able to remove users from the account, and thus the Trust Log, without full freedom to rewrite World State arbitrarily.
L92: For scenarios like this, the system defines server Trust Log entries and a small, fixed set of server Operations the service may apply at any time. Those Operations never add new non-server key material. A malicious or mistaken server entry would be visible in the log and would at worst disrupt service, not undermine the Trust Log’s goal of guaranteeing the authenticity of public keys used to share sensitive data without needing to trust 1Password’s servers.
L93: ## The Trust Log in automated provisioning
L94: 
L95: The Trust Log is part of what makes 【1†automated provisioning】 in 1Password possible. Any provisioning flow can grant access to secrets. In 1Password, access is granted by encrypting secrets with the public key of the user or group that needs access. The key used in that encryption must belong to the intended recipient, or the secret could be compromised.
L96: Together with the 【9†confidential computing platform】, the Trust Log lets the enclave that manages provisioned access to groups and shared vaults authenticate the public keys it grants access to. Neither 1Password, nor someone with infrastructure access, can trick the service into granting access to a key that isn’t part of the account.
